title: Balanced Brackets
directAnswer: Scan the string once with a stack. Push every opening bracket; on a closing bracket, the stack top must be the exact matching opener — pop it, otherwise the string is unbalanced. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time, O(n) space. The naive 'repeatedly delete (), [], {} until nothing changes' works but is O(n²).

rules: Three failure modes, all must be checked: **wrong** match, closer with an **empty** stack, and leftover **openers** at the end.
On a closer, an empty stack means a closer with no partner — return false immediately, don't pop.
Map each closer to its opener (`)`→`(`, `]`→`[`, `}`→`{`) so the match is one comparison, not a chain of `if`s.
The stack must be **empty** at the end. `"((("` never hits a mismatch but is still unbalanced.
Odd length can be rejected in O(1) — an odd number of characters can never pair up.
whenToUse: Matching nested pairs where the most recent open must close first
Validating brackets, tags, or any LIFO 'open then close' structure
Parsing / expression evaluation where you track depth
Any 'undo the last thing first' requirement
antiSignals: Only ONE type of bracket → a single counter (int) beats a stack, O(1) space
Pairs can close in any order, not LIFO → counting, not a stack
No nesting at all → simple equality of open/close counts
remember.takeaway: A stack is the data structure for 'the most recently opened thing must close first'. Once you see brackets, HTML tags, or nested scopes, reach for it — the same shape powers Min Stack, Valid Parentheses, and recursive-call simulation.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise LIFO matching and pick a stack — and whether you remember all three ways the string can be invalid, not just a wrong-pair mismatch.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to check the stack is empty at the end (so '(((' passes), or popping from an empty stack on a stray closer like ']'.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Mention the O(1) odd-length rejection, map closers to openers instead of a chain of ifs, and name the LIFO insight explicitly.

problemStatement:
A bracket is any one of `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, or `]`. Two brackets are a **matched pair** when an opening bracket occurs to the left of a closing bracket of the **exact same type**.

Given a string `s` containing only these six characters, determine whether the sequence is **balanced**: every opening bracket has a corresponding closing bracket of the same type, and pairs are properly nested (the most recently opened bracket is the first one closed).

Return `true` if balanced, `false` otherwise.
constraints: s consists only of the characters ()[]{}
An empty inner sequence is fine — '()' is balanced
Return a boolean (some variants ask for the string 'YES'/'NO')
understanding: Each closing bracket must cancel the bracket opened most recently — that's last-in-first-out, which is exactly a stack. The string is balanced only if every closer cancels the correct opener AND nothing is left open at the end.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the string contain characters other than the six brackets?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per the constraints, no. If it could, decide whether to ignore non-brackets or reject — say it out loud.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the empty string balanced?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Conventionally yes (nothing is unmatched), but the constraint here says length ≥ 1, so you won't hit it. Confirm the convention anyway.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do different bracket types interleave, like '([)]'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: That is NOT balanced — the ')' tries to close a '[' that is still open. The stack catches this automatically.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Return a boolean or a 'YES'/'NO' string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Depends on the platform. The logic is identical; just format the output at the end.

examples.explanation: Perfectly nested: ( ) closes, then [ ] closes, then { } closes — stack drains cleanly.
The ')' arrives while '[' is on top of the stack. ')' expects '(' but sees '[' → mismatch.
No mismatch ever occurs, but three openers are left on the stack at the end → unbalanced.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Repeated Pair Deletion
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to show you understand the structure, then immediately note it is O(n²) and reach for the stack.
hints: A balanced string can always be collapsed by repeatedly removing an innermost empty pair like '()', '[]', or '{}'. What's left after removing all of them?
Keep replacing every occurrence of '()', '[]', '{}' with nothing, in a loop, until the string stops changing.
If the final string is empty, it was balanced. If something non-empty remains, it wasn't. Each full pass is O(n) and you may need O(n) passes.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each deletion pass scans the whole string (O(n)) and may remove only one layer of pairs, so up to n/2 passes → O(n²) total. The intermediate string copies cost O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The defining property of a balanced bracket string is that it is built entirely from innermost empty pairs. `"{[()]}"` contains `"()"`; delete it and you get `"{[]}"`, which contains `"[]"`; delete that and you get `"{}"`; delete that and you get `""`. Reaching the empty string means balanced.

**Why repeated deletion works.** Every matched pair, by definition, surrounds a (possibly empty) balanced substring. The *innermost* pairs have nothing between them, so they appear literally as `"()"`, `"[]"`, or `"{}"`. Removing them exposes the next layer out, and the process repeats. If the string is balanced, every character eventually disappears.

**Why a single pass is not enough.** One sweep removes only the pairs that are *currently* adjacent. After removal, brand-new adjacencies form — the `"[]"` in `"{[]}"` only became adjacent after `"()"` was gone. So you must loop until a full pass changes nothing.

**Why we don't ship this.** Each pass is O(n), and a deeply nested string like `"((((....))))"` peels one layer per pass, giving O(n) passes and O(n²) total. For n = 10⁵ that's 10¹⁰ operations — far too slow. It's a great way to *explain* what balanced means, but the stack does the same job in one pass.
approaches.insight: This approach reveals the recursive structure of balanced strings — they collapse from the inside out. The stack is just a way to do all of that collapsing in a single left-to-right pass instead of repeated rescans.

dryRun.intro: Repeatedly delete any '()', '[]', '{}' until the string is stable. Balanced iff we reach empty.

java.explanation: Remember the string before this pass so we can detect when nothing changes.
Strip every adjacent empty pair. Each replace is O(n) and builds a new string.
Keep looping until a full pass removes nothing — that's the fixed point.
Empty means every bracket was paired away → balanced.

python.explanation: Loop until a pass leaves the string unchanged.
str.replace builds a new string each call — this is what makes it O(n²).
Balanced exactly when nothing is left.

pitfalls: Doing a single replace pass instead of looping — '{[]}' wouldn't fully collapse.
Using this on large inputs — O(n²) times out at n = 10⁵.
Forgetting that string replace allocates a new string each time, hiding extra cost.

approaches.name: Stack — One Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'the most recent opener must match this closer' — LIFO — not just 'use a stack'.
hints: When you see a closing bracket, which opening bracket must it match? The one opened most recently and not yet closed. What structure gives you 'most recent, not yet handled' in O(1)?
Push every opener onto a stack. On a closer, the correct partner is whatever is on top — pop it and verify it's the right type.
Three ways to fail: the stack is empty when a closer arrives (no partner), the popped opener is the wrong type (mismatch), or the stack is non-empty at the end (unclosed openers).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once → O(n) total work. The stack holds at most n/2 openers → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the string once. Push every opening bracket. When you hit a closing bracket, the only valid partner is the bracket on top of the stack — pop it and check the types match. After the scan, the stack must be empty.

**The LIFO insight that picks the structure.** In `"{[()]}"`, when `)` arrives the open bracket that *must* close is `(` — the one opened most recently. Not `{`, not `[`. 'Most recently opened, not yet closed' is the literal definition of a stack's top. That single observation is why a stack, and nothing simpler, fits: brackets nest, and nesting is last-in-first-out.

**Why three separate failure checks, not one.** A balanced string can break in three distinct ways, and a correct solution catches all three:

- **Stray closer:** `"]"` or `")("`. A closer arrives but the stack is empty — there is no opener to match. If you blindly `pop()` here, Java throws and Python errors. Check `empty` *before* popping.
- **Wrong pair:** `"(]"`. The stack top is `(` but the closer is `]`. Pop, compare types, fail on mismatch.
- **Leftover openers:** `"((("`. No mismatch ever happens, but the loop ends with three `(` still on the stack. The final `stack.isEmpty()` check is the only thing that catches this — forgetting it is the single most common bug on this problem.

**Why map closers to openers.** Instead of a tangle of `if (c == ')' && top == '(') ...`, build a tiny map `) → (`, `] → [`, `} → {`. On a closer, look up its required opener and compare against the popped value in one line. Cleaner, and it generalises if more pair types appear.

**The O(1) early reject.** A balanced string has even length — every bracket is half of a pair. If `s.length()` is odd you can return `false` before scanning a single character. Small, but it signals you think about invariants.
approaches.insight: The stack literally *is* the list of currently-open brackets, innermost on top. Reading the stack at any moment tells you exactly which scopes are still open — that's why the same pattern simulates nested function calls, HTML/XML tag validation, and depth tracking in parsers.

dryRun.intro: Push openers; on each closer the stack top must be its exact partner. Stack must end empty.

java.explanation: Odd length can never pair up — O(1) early reject.
Closer → required opener, so matching is one comparison instead of a chain of ifs.
ArrayDeque is the modern stack in Java — faster than the legacy Stack class.
Openers go on the stack to wait for their partner.
Check empty FIRST (stray closer), then pop and compare (wrong pair). Short-circuit avoids popping an empty stack.
Leftover openers like '(((' mean unbalanced — this final check is the one people forget.

python.explanation: Odd-length strings can't be balanced — return early.
Map each closer to the opener it requires.
A Python list is the idiomatic stack — append/pop operate on the end in O(1).
Membership in the opener string classifies the character.

python.line: elif not stack or stack.pop() != match[c]:
python.explanation: Empty stack (stray closer) OR wrong popped opener both fail. 'not stack' is checked first so pop never hits an empty list.
Empty stack at the end means everything matched.

diagrams.title: Stack contents through the scan
diagrams.caption: Top of stack is the rightmost element. Watch it grow on openers and shrink on closers.

edgeCases.behavior: First char is a closer with an empty stack → return false without popping. The stack.isEmpty() guard prevents a crash.
Three pushes, no closer, loop ends with a non-empty stack → final isEmpty() check returns false.
')' arrives with '[' on top → match.get(')') is '(' ≠ '[' → false. Interleaving is caught automatically.

pitfalls: Popping before checking the stack is empty — crashes on a stray closer like ']'.
Omitting the final empty check — '(((' slips through as 'balanced'.
Using a chain of equality ifs instead of a closer→opener map — verbose and bug-prone.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the final 'stack must be empty' check, so unclosed openers like '(((' pass.
Popping from an empty stack when a closing bracket appears first.
Comparing a closer to the wrong opener type — not mapping ) → (, ] → [, } → {.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the end-of-scan empty check
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A string of only openers, like '(((', never triggers a mismatch — the bug only shows up if you verify the stack is empty after the loop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Popping before checking emptiness
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A closer arriving first (']' or ')(' ) means the stack is empty. Calling pop() on it throws NoSuchElementException in Java and IndexError in Python.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if stack.pop() != match[c]:  # crashes when stack is empty
    return False
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if not stack or stack.pop() != match[c]:
    return False

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Hard-coded if-chain instead of a map
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Manually pairing each closer with each opener is verbose and easy to get wrong; a closer→opener map reduces it to a single lookup and comparison.
